name: Portal page
description: The screens a supplier signs in to: the orders you have placed with them, the acknowledgement, an invoice against a receipt, what has been paid, and their own details. One vendor is the whole application, and the layout is built to make that visible.
when_to_use: A party outside the company — a supplier, a transporter, a contractor — signed in to a URL you gave them, working on the records you share with them and on nothing else. The decision this entry turns on is that it deliberately does not use app-shell, and it is the only signed-in layout in the system that does not, so say what that costs: no command palette, no keyboard shortcuts, no collapsing rail, no nav landmark with thirty destinations under it, no live counts down the side. Every one of those is right for a buyer who is in the console six hours a day and was trained on it for a morning, and every one of them is furniture for a supplier who has four destinations, signs in four times a month, will never be trained, and has three other customers' portals open in other tabs. What replaces the shell is a slim header carrying both company names and four links, and that header is the entire navigation — do not wrap this in app-shell, and do not grow a sidebar onto it later, because the day a portal needs a sidebar it has become a second console and the fix is to take screens away rather than to add chrome. Signing in is auth-page and nothing here reinvents it: the portal reuses that screen with its own next, and a portal that draws a second sign-in form is two credential paths to keep patched and two places to get the timing leak wrong. Against index-page and record-page — those are the internal screens for these same purchase orders, and the portal cannot just show them. They carry the cost centre, the buyer's notes, the approval route, the rate history, the other vendors' quotations against the same enquiry, and a filter band built for a register of 1,438 rows; a supplier has four rows, may see none of that, and does not know the words. Reach for index-page and record-page inside the console and for this outside it, and never for one URL that serves both with the sensitive regions behind a template condition: the queryset behind that page was never scoped, and one missed condition publishes the lot.
rules: This is the one signed-in layout that renders outside app-shell, and the header in the shell variant is the whole of the chrome it replaces. Two things the shell owns still have to exist here and are drawn on the page: the skip link, first in the DOM, and a real <main> landmark for it to reach. The rest of what app-shell carries — the palette, the shortcuts, the rail, the counts — is dropped on purpose, and the test for adding any of it back is whether a supplier who has used the portal twice would find it without being told.

Scope is the security model, and the screen says so rather than looking like a register that happens to be short today. One sentence under the h1 names both parties and states the boundary — this portal holds the orders between Konspec and Gujarat Polymers, and nothing else. It is a sentence and not a filter chip: a chip implies something that can be removed, and this cannot be. The same sentence is what stops a supplier who sees four rows from concluding that the fifth order was lost.

The scoping itself lives in the view and never in the template. Every queryset in the portal starts filtered to the signed-in contact's vendor before anything else touches it, and a template is not allowed to widen it. A template condition is a display rule that a designer will move; a queryset filter is the boundary, and the difference only shows up the first time somebody adds a column.

Two names, one job each. Konspec on the left is the system of record — it says whose numbering, whose terms and whose figures these are. The vendor on the right is the account — it is the check a person makes when they have three customers' portals open and want to know they are typing into the right one. Neither is a logo slot. avatar's rule holds: nothing in this system uploads a picture, an organisation takes rounded-lg where a person takes rounded-full, and a logo arrives at whatever size the vendor emailed it and takes the header height with it.

Their reference sits beside ours on every row and in every heading. PO-2026-0418 means nothing inside Gujarat Polymers; GP/SO/2026/1184 is what their sales office and their accounts clerk search on, and an invoice query that quotes only our number costs a phone call at both ends. It is a column on the list and a line under the heading on every record, and it is theirs to set — the portal shows it back, it does not own it.

No internal vocabulary anywhere on these screens. GRN is a delivery receipt, an indent is nothing they need to hear about, a cost centre is never mentioned, and Approved is meaningless because it does not say approved by whom or what it means for them. The words that survive are the ones a supplier already uses: order, delivery, receipt, invoice, payment. Where a Konspec number has to appear because it will be quoted back — the receipt number, the invoice reference — it is labelled with what it is rather than with what we call it.

The status pill is badge's shape unchanged and the dot keeps its locked colour; what changes is the word, and the word says what the record is doing to them rather than what it is doing to us. Waiting on the supplier is the amber dot, an order running normally is the zinc dot, a delivery past its promised date is the red dot, and a finished one is emerald. The mapping is fixed in the anatomy so two portal screens cannot describe the same state differently.

Each screen does one thing, and the acknowledgement is the proof. It is not the order page with a button on it — it is a page whose whole content is one question, the facts needed to answer it, and the answer. The single most valuable thing a supplier portal does is turn a promised date into a date both sides agreed on, and it does not survive being the fourth control on a record page.

The restricted screen is one screen for two different server answers, and that is the point of it. A record that belongs to another vendor and a record that was never raised return the same page and the same status code, so the URL space cannot be walked to find out which of our suppliers exists or how many orders we place. It says as much in words — this portal answers the same way either way — because a user who is not told that will keep trying.

It keeps the portal header, which is where it parts company with error-page. error-page drops the chrome because there is no working page left to hang it on; here the portal is working perfectly and the header is the supplier's only navigation, so dropping it strands somebody who mistyped a URL with nothing but the browser back button. Everything else about that screen is error-page's: graphite icon well, the status label above the heading, the h1 as a sentence, one primary route back and one human to ask.

A change to the supplier's own details is submitted, not applied. The current value stays on screen as the value in force, and the requested change sits under it in a recessed band saying what was asked for, when, and what has to happen before it takes effect. Applying it optimistically and reverting on rejection is the version that ships fraud: a bank account change is the single most attacked field in any procurement system, so the screen states the verification — a call to the number already on the account — and states that nobody from Konspec will ever ask for that confirmation by email.

An invoice that does not match the receipt is accepted and held, not rejected. Blocking the submit sends the supplier to the telephone and leaves us with no record of what they think they are owed; taking it and holding it puts the disagreement in the system where a buyer can settle it. So the mismatch is stated before the submit, in figures and in days, with the note field beside it already labelled for the explanation.

Sign out is a form POST carrying a CSRF token, never a link. Django's LogoutView has refused GET since 4.1, and a GET sign-out is fired by link prefetchers and by the mail scanners that follow every URL in a notification — the supplier is then signed out by an email nobody has opened.

The phone arrangement is not an afterthought here, and it is a different arrangement rather than a reflow. Suppliers open this on a phone far more often than our own staff open the console on one: the four destinations become a four-across row of labelled tiles under the header instead of a link bar, the list becomes cards ordered by what needs them rather than by date, and the one action on the card that is waiting is a full-width 40px target.

Each variant root here is a bounded preview — h-[640px] with a rounded-xl border — so a whole screen renders in a box on this page. As a real page, drop the wrapper height and border, put bg-zinc-100 on <body>, and let the header stick to the viewport rather than to the wrapper. Ids are prefixed per variant because every variant of this entry renders on one documentation page, and two screens sharing pp-main means the skip link lands on whichever one the parser saw first.

anatomy.description: A single white band: Konspec's mark and name on the left, the vendor's mark, name and signed-in contact on the right, and Sign out as a form POST. Not a topbar — no search, no notifications, no palette trigger.

Four links and no more, in navigation-menu's link-bar shape, with aria-current="page" on the one you are on. Four is the budget: a fifth destination is a screen that should have been merged into one of the four. It appears on the four destinations and not on the two task screens reached from them — a nav bar over a half-answered form is four ways to lose what was typed, and those screens carry a back link instead.
On the acknowledgement and the invoice, above the h1: one route, to the list the task was reached from. It replaces the destination bar rather than joining it.

One sentence under the h1 naming both parties and stating that this is the whole of what the account reaches. Prose, not a chip and not a filter pill, because it describes a boundary rather than a choice.
Our number and the material, their reference, the value, the promised date, and the ask. The ask is the column that makes the screen worth opening.

The status pill plus the one thing we are waiting for, and the link that does it. badge's pill unchanged: bg-zinc-200, ring-zinc-300, zinc-700 text, and only the dot carries the colour — amber waiting on the supplier, zinc running normally, red past the promised date, emerald finished.
A fieldset whose legend is the question in full, two radios, and the follow-up fields under the option that opens them. One question per screen.
On the invoice screen: the receipt value, the invoice value and the difference between them, restated in words as what will happen. Never a blocking validation error.
A bg-zinc-50 band under the value in force, carrying what was asked for, when it was sent, and what has to happen before it applies. The value above it does not move until then.
The named buyer at Konspec with an email address and a direct number. It is the escape hatch for everything the four screens do not do, and it is a person rather than a mailbox.

behaviour: The header is the only navigation on every screen, including the restricted one. Nothing here opens off-canvas, so there is no focus trap to manage and no state to persist.

The order list is not searched, filtered or sorted. Four rows do not need a filter band, and a band that never changes anything teaches a supplier that this portal is the same kind of thing as the console.

The acknowledgement offers two answers. Accepting the promised date submits on its own; proposing a different one reveals a date, a reason and a note, and those controls are disabled while they are hidden so a proposal abandoned halfway is not posted with the acceptance.

The invoice screen compares the amount typed against the value of the receipt it is being raised against, on every keystroke, and states the difference in rupees and the consequence in working days. It never disables the submit.

A change to bank details, tax registration or a contact is submitted for checking. The current value stays in force and on screen; the pending band under it says what was asked and what happens next, and it clears when Konspec accepts or rejects it, never when the page reloads.

The restricted screen renders for a record belonging to another vendor and for a record that does not exist, with the same words and the same status code, so the two cannot be told apart from outside.

Below md the order table is replaced by cards carrying the same fields in the same order, and at 390px the destination bar becomes four labelled tiles. Nothing on any of these screens scrolls sideways.

Every figure is tabular-nums and every rupee amount is grouped the Indian way, because the supplier is reconciling these against their own ledger and a mis-grouped lakh is the sort of thing that gets read as a rate dispute.
accessibility: The skip link is first in the DOM and <main> carries tabindex="-1", because app-shell normally provides both and this layout does not use it. Without the tabindex the fragment scrolls the page and leaves the keyboard at the top of the document.

One <main> and one <h1> per screen, and the h1 names the screen rather than the company — the company is in the header, on every screen, and repeating it as the heading wastes the one landmark a screen-reader user navigates by.

The destination bar is a <nav> with an accessible name and the current destination carries aria-current="page". The tint is what a sighted user sees; the attribute is what everyone else gets, and writing only the tint gives half the users nothing.

The scope sentence is ordinary prose in the document rather than a live region or an alert. It is true on every load and never changes, and a role="status" on a permanent sentence is announced on arrival at every screen.

The acknowledgement is a fieldset whose legend is the whole question, so the question is read once on entry rather than once per arrow key, and the follow-up fields are described by their own message paragraphs with stable ids.

The conditional fields are bound :disabled to the inverse of the condition that shows them. display:none does not remove a control from the POST or from constraint validation, so a hidden required field makes the form unsubmittable with nothing on screen explaining why.
The match line on the invoice screen is pointed at by aria-describedby from the amount field, so the constraint is read when focus lands rather than only being visible beside it.
The restricted screen carries no role="alert". It arrives as a full document load, the <title> states it first, and a live region present at first paint announces nothing anyway.

Both renderings of the order list — the table above md and the cards below it — are in the DOM at once, so neither carries a form control with a name. A display:none input still posts, and two renderings of one row post that row twice.

Every action is a real <a> or <button> with a name that says what it does in the supplier's words — Acknowledge this order, Send your invoice — and wears focus-visible:outline-3 focus-visible:outline-offset-2. No rings anywhere.

Every queryset starts here. Nothing in portal/templates may widen it: a template condition is a display rule and somebody will move it, and the page still renders perfectly the day they do. """ def get_vendor(self): return self.request.user.supplier_contact.vendor def get_queryset(self): return super().get_queryset().filter(vendor=self.get_vendor()) class OrderList(VendorScopedMixin, ListView): model = PurchaseOrder context_object_name = 'orders' template_name = 'portal/orders.html' def get_queryset(self): return (super().get_queryset() .exclude(status=PurchaseOrder.DRAFT) .select_related('receipt') .order_by('-raised_on')) def get_context_data(self, **kw): return super().get_context_data(vendor=self.get_vendor(), **kw) class OrderDetail(VendorScopedMixin, DetailView): model = PurchaseOrder # 404 and not 403. A 403 on another supplier's order and a 404 on an # order that was never raised is an enumeration oracle: outside the # company it leaks who we buy from and how much we buy. get_object() # on the scoped queryset raises Http404 for both, which is the # restricted variant of this entry. A draft order is excluded here as well as scoped. Draft is our word for an order that has not been signed off internally, and a supplier who is emailed about one and then finds it withdrawn has been told something that was not a commitment. supplier_status and supplier_next_step are model properties, not template logic.
